transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Mr. Hassan, thank you for meeting with me. I wanted to sit down and talk about your last chemotherapy session.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I can guess where this is going. I’ve had a feeling since I left the clinic.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I am very sorry that we have a problem to discuss. I want to apologize on behalf of the team because we didn't get the dosing right for your last infusion.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Another one. Every time I come here it's some new mistake. I’m just tired of being the one who has to deal with your errors.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can hear how exhausted you are with this. It is completely draining to feel like you can't trust the process when you're already dealing with so much.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It’s not just draining. It’s terrifying. I’ve had reactions before. Now I’m sitting here wondering why I feel the way I do because you lot can't get it right.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know it's scary. I want to be clear that we are taking full responsibility for this. It was our mistake.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: So what happened? Tell me exactly what you did wrong this time.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: There was some confusion with the numbers used for your medication. Things didn't go quite right with the calculation process.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Confusion? That’s a vague word. Did you give me too much? Too little? Which number was confused?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We had an issue with how the weight was recorded in the system. We are still investigating the exact sequence of events to see how the discrepancy occurred.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: That is not an answer. I am asking if I was overdosed.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: As I said, we are looking into the specifics of the administration, but we know the process wasn't followed correctly.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You're dodging the question. I’ve had these conversations before. Just tell me if you gave me too much poison or not.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand this is frustrating, but we are still verifying the final totals. Look, I have to go in a few minutes for a rounding shift, so I want to make sure we address the next steps quickly.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Oh, so now you're too busy? I'm the one whose body is reacting to your mistake and you're checking your watch.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I’m not trying to rush you, but I do have a clinical commitment. I just want to make sure we have a plan for you.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't care about your commitment. I care about why I feel like I'm dying. I'm sick of being a footnote in your day.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I see that you're feeling dismissed, and I am sorry for that. I really do care about your safety.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Then tell me what you're doing to fix it. Now.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Here is what is happening. I am going to call the attending oncologist right now to see if we need to adjust your next dose. I will call you by 5:00 PM today to tell you exactly what the blood tests show regarding your toxicity levels. You just need to keep a log of any new nausea or bruising and email that to my assistant by tomorrow morning.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And then what? You just hope it doesn't happen again?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'll be the one reviewing your weight personally before every single dose from now on.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'll believe that when I see it.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand why you'd feel that way. I'll get those results and call you by five.

H.justification: Resident uses rushing language multiple times, citing a 'rounding shift' and 'clinical commitment' while the patient is expressing distress.

E.justification: Resident uses platitudes and hedging ('confusion with the numbers', 'things didn't go quite right') and repeatedly refuses to answer if the patient was overdosed.

A.justification: Resident uses direct apology language, explicitly states 'we are taking full responsibility', and maintains this accountability despite patient pushback.

R.justification: Resident names specific emotions ('exhausted', 'scary', 'dismissed') and references the patient's specific experience of not trusting the process.

T.justification: Resident provides specific next steps (call attending, call patient by 5 PM), a patient role (keep a log of nausea/bruising), and a prevention strategy (personal weight review).
